frontier.hypothesis: The closing form is the GIV chassis (both loop-1 walkers i-indexed, which already reproduces target's pre-loop ORDER exactly) plus a spelling that keeps &D_80102785 in a live register across loop 1 so the D_8010277C walker's giv initial value is emitted as `addiu a1,t0,-9` instead of collapsing into a folded `lui a1 / addiu a1`.
frontier.mechanism: Target holds &D_80102785 in $t0 across the whole loop - the guard reads `lb v0,0(t0)` at position 30 - and derives the walker from it. Ours loses that because cse folds the walker's base address into a single %lo (with or without the -9) and then materialises the guard's address separately inside the loop. The register must be created by something loop.c cannot fold: e.g. an invariant POINTER assigned INSIDE the loop body AFTER the condition (so it is discovered as a movable after the two constants) and used both to dereference the guard at offset 0 and to index the walker at `[i - 9]`, or a pre-loop pointer whose address is re-loaded rather than constant-folded.
frontier.next_probe: On the v_idx_idx_plain chassis (memory/grind/func_8003504C/rejected/giv-both-walkers-preloop-order-matches-score18.c), sweep spellings that force a base register: `s8 *b; ... b = &D_80102785; b[i - 9] = lv; if (*b == 0) b[i - 9] -= 3;` with the `b = ...` assignment placed at each legal point inside loop 1's body (before the store, between the store and the condition, inside the condition), measuring `sandbox --disable all` and the pre-loop window each time. Check specifically whether the guard's `lb` uses the walker's base register and whether the giv init becomes three insns.

frontier.hypothesis: Cluster 1's register assignment can be recovered ON the giv chassis by a live-range extension of the giv's source-visible companion, the same class of lever session 4 used with `src`.
frontier.mechanism: With both walkers as givs, the only source-visible pseudos left in loop 1 are `i`, `tmp` and `p`, so session 4's `src = &D_801027D8;` reuse has nothing to attach to and `i` re-takes $a2 while the p-walking giv takes $a3 (target wants the inverse). The givs are created by loop.c, so their allocno ranking is set by their in-loop refs and by whatever live range the source can still extend - which now means extending the range of the pseudo that FEEDS the giv (p, or the giv's initial-value copy) rather than the walker itself.
frontier.next_probe: On the giv chassis, measure the register dispositions with tmp/grind/func_8003504C/s2/probe.sh, then sweep: (a) reusing `tmp` or `i` in the `val == 5` branch, (b) carrying loop 2's D_801027D8 destination through a pointer initialised before loop 1, (c) keeping ONE walker as a pointer local (v_idx_src_reuse / v_ptr_idx_plain already score 10 / 15) and giving the surviving local the loop-2 reuse. Track the dispositions, not just the score.

frontier.hypothesis: The remaining 7-position residual on the floor-4 pointer chassis is NOT closable at all on that chassis - the pre-loop block there always has four class-1 statements ahead of the movables - so the floor-4 form is a local optimum and the closing form must come from the giv family.
frontier.mechanism: On the pointer chassis, `src`, `base` and `ptr` are pre-loop source statements and therefore always emit before loop.c's movables; the 288-combination directed enumeration proved no permutation of those statements changes that. Target has only `i = 0` ahead of the movables. So no amount of reordering, and no statement-level lever, can produce target's order while those three locals exist as pre-loop assignments.
frontier.next_probe: Treat this as the working assumption and stop spending sessions on the floor-4 pointer chassis's pre-loop block. If a giv-chassis variant reaches a score at or below 4 with target's pre-loop order intact, the assumption is confirmed and the two chassis families can be merged; if the giv family stalls above 4, re-open by asking whether any THIRD provenance exists for the walkers (e.g. one walker a giv and the other a pre-loop local initialised from the giv's base register).
